items.title: Peace bonds: The colonial tool rearing its head amid protests in 2026
items.summary: In 2023, the Indian parliament enacted three new penal laws: the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in place of its colonial era ancestors, a move that Union Home Minister Amit Shah said would make the criminal justice system "completely Swadeshi" . Back then, lawyers criticised the "new" statues as "old wine in a new bottle", largely retaining many problematic provisions introduced in colonial times. In 2026, the means adopted by the British Raj of quelling dissent still remain firmly cemented in Indian penal procedures. The recent nationwide protests and the police response to them put these provisions under the spotlight, especially those that deal with preventive policing. Detained protestors were made to sign bonds promising not to cause "breach of peace" for varying amounts of time. Here, we give historical context to these peace bonds, show how they have been retained in current jurisprudence and speak to leading criminal law practitioners on the issue.
